messages.subject: Re: Geomorph query
parts:
Hi Aaron,

I am going to share this with our geomorph package group, as there are some important conceptual points I think we can all benefit from.  Thank you for allowing me to share.  Your queries do not border on moronic but your attempts to solve your analytical problem do offer a square peg - round hole scenario that we can all learn from.

First, a technical comment.  It’s a bit hard to tell without the actual data but a few things spring to mind.  First, it looks like your input variables has different numbers of specimens.  I’m guessing your phylogeny has 83 species?  I’m guessing also that you have 2049 specimens?  When doing PGLS, you need a data set that has rows equal to the number of taxa in your phylogeny.  Second, and especially if the first issue is not an issue, the immense number of interactions you have is neither computationally manageable nor practical, even if it were manageable.  Your variables are continuous variables.  It only makes sense to set up interactions between factors or factors and covariates (not between covariates and other covariates, as you have done).  The design matrix for you analysis must be so huge that you run out of degrees of freedom pretty fast.  The simple answer is, don’t do this.

However, and this is where we can all benefit, you should not be forcing this analysis into a multiple regression analysis, anyway.  I think what your reviewer is suggesting is that you have boiled a complex trait - shape - down into a number of PCs that you treat independently.  This is not appropriate.  Shape is a multidimensional trait that requires a full set of variables - not a portion via rotation, like PCA - in order to have a direct meaning with the set of landmarks you chose to define shape.  The "multivariate PGLS” suggestion might refer to a multiple regression design but it can also refer to any multivariate covariation analysis, which allows for PGLS estimation of coefficients rather than OLS.  I recommend that you abandon the multiple regression approach and use a two-block partial least squares (PLS) approach.  The latter is a multivariate generalization of Pearson’s correlation rather than a multivariate generalization of multiple regression.  The PLS approach is simple and gives you the answer you want: are my two data sets integrated (correlated)?.  The geomorph function, phylo.integration allows one to do this with PGLS.

But more than this, I want to draw your attention to our (Dean Adams and I) recent paper in Evolution: D.C. Adams and M.L. Collyer. 2016. On the comparison of the strength of morphological integration across morphometric datasets. Evolution. 70:2623-2631.

In it, we describe a method for comparing the effect sizes for different comparisons of integration, allowing one to determine if two components (among several) are more integrated than others.  From the look of it, you have animal prey (I assume a matrix of proportions?  If this is a distance matrix, one can use principal coordinates.), body shape (use the whole matrix, not PCs), tooth characteristics (make a matrix of just these), and “other”?  (Nor sure what the other measures besides intestine length are.  It is perfectly fine to have a matrix with only one variable though, if these should be treated separately.)

So, you can perform an integration test on each pairwise match of matrices; e.g., body shape/prey, tooth/prey; and you can also do the same with the “predictors” if you like; e.g., body shape/tooth.  If you save these with names (e.g., test12, test13, test23), you can then run comapre.pls, our geomorph function for the test we describe in the paper; e.g., compare.pls(test12, test13, test23).  In the process you will ascertain if prey size is correlated with the various characteristics and with which characteristic, the effect is stronger.  I think this is exactly what you want to answer and it also does exactly what the reviewers requested.

The help files for these functions should get you going, but feel free to send me an email if you hit a snag.  

As another word of caution - again, this can benefit everyone - if one wants to force the multiple regression approach, the * in your equation should be changed to + with an understanding that the R^2 from the analysis is analogous to the square of r from the PLS approach, as if the second matrix is a combination of PCs1-4 for shape, plus the other variables, which might not make much sense.  You could posit that this is okay, and by looking at the coefficients or effect R^2 or Z-scores, one can ascertain which variables are most important.  However, be aware that procD.pgls uses type I (sequential sums of squares), which means variable order matters.  The effect of one variable can only be evaluated with an understanding that the other variables proceeding it have already been accounted for.  To evaluate the importance of every effect, given all the other effects, one must use advanced.procD.lm and evaluate each variable, one by one, using a combination of a model with all effects and one minus the “target” effect.  I do not recommend this as the best course of action, but it can be done.

I hope this was helpful!

Mike

On Dec 17, 2016, at 5:34 AM, Davis, Aaron <aaron...@jcu.edu.au> wrote:

Thanks for the prompt response Mike, 
and if I'm imposing on some holiday time or something similar, it can certainly wait (and if anything I ask is more broadly useful to others, go for it, hopefully some of my queries don't border on moronic). As a bit of context, I just got some reviews back on a manuscript where I tested the association between proportion of animal prey in diet against the first few PCs synthesizing major axes of morphological variation in a fish clade. So it was basically univariate PGLS in CAPER on individual PC axis scores and diet (and some additional pgls on specific traits and diet). One reviewer suggested the use of PCA outputs was obscuring the specific traits primarily driving some of the significant diet-morphology co-variations I identified (which may have some credence in retrospect). They suggested I use multivariate PGLS (I presume on the collective raw trait data), instead of assessing each PC separately in a univariate framework.

So I guess I want to identify a specific subset of the best predictor variables from a larger set. I've been doing some preliminary analyses with procD.pgls in Geomorph just to familiarise myself with things, but I don't suppose you have an example worked up somewhere I could use as a guide (some of the examples you posted on R bloggers on other geomorph applications have been great)? I'm a bit uncertain on how to exactly frame up the model formulas for example (or assess the relative importance each predictor in the model). I've also managed to hit some sort of glitch when I try to run procD.pgls on my entire dataset (it seems to run fine for up to six input variables with interactions). I've included my script and error message below (which may provide some insights).


> terap.pgls2 <- procD.pgls(animalprey ~ jawCLR*intestineL*jawOLR*PC1BodyShape*PC2BodyShape*PC3BodyShape*PC4BodyShape*ToothSpacing*ToothHeight*PC1tooth*PC2tooth, phy = tree, iter = 999, RRPP=FALSE)
  |=================================================================================================| 100%
Error in data.frame(df, SS, MS, Rsq = R2, F = Fs) : 
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 2049, 83
In addition: Warning message:
In SS/df : longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length


A lot of this confusion I'm sure stems from some lack of familiarity with multiple regression, but any tips/examples on how to work through this would be greatly appreciated. And thanks for you time.
cheers
